purpose: Reusable structural-containment rules for candidate V2 object-first prompt compilation. Each rule changes SCENE DESIGN itself (what is structurally present or absent in the scene) rather than merely appending a 'no humans' negative to an otherwise human-centered scene. Rules are referenced by id from object_first_rules_v2.json's archetype_defaults / id_prefix_overrides. This spec is read-only input for a future V2 compiler; it does not generate prompts or images by itself.

action_aftermath.bad_pattern: Equipment shown dynamically in use mid-action (e.g. shoes mid-stride), which reliably pulls a human body part (legs, hands, arms) into frame even when a human is never explicitly requested.
action_aftermath.good_pattern: Design the scene as the moment immediately AFTER the action: equipment at rest, fresh physical traces (footprints, chalk dust, displaced material, a still-ticking stopwatch, settling water/dust), no currently-moving body part attached to anything.
action_aftermath.notes: The energy of the card must come from the aftermath details, not from an implied currently-acting body.

private_empty_venue.bad_pattern: A public/social venue (cafe, restaurant, tavern, arena concourse) used as the backdrop, which reliably causes the model to populate the background with patrons, staff, or spectators even when not requested.
private_empty_venue.good_pattern: Relocate the scene to a private, empty version of the same venue type (a private game room instead of a cafe; an empty street food stall instead of a busy one; an empty overlook instead of a scenic viewpoint with tourists) so no social context is structurally implied.
private_empty_venue.notes: This is the single most impactful containment rule found across all four rounds - the venue choice, not the hero object, was the actual leak source in every case it was applied to.

object_hero_no_performer.bad_pattern: A scene built around 'a performer doing X with an instrument/tool', where the performer is the implicit subject even if described only via the instrument.
object_hero_no_performer.good_pattern: Make the instrument/tool itself the sole hero, staged mid-resonance or mid-use through purely physical/optical cues (a spotlight on piano keys with faint string-vibration suggestion; a lens reflecting a landscape) with no performer present at all.
object_hero_no_performer.notes: This is a lower-risk rule than action_aftermath or private_empty_venue - both validating cases passed cleanly on the first attempt without needing a round-4 redesign.

abstract_system_no_operator.bad_pattern: A 'person operating equipment' scene (coder at a monitor, hands adjusting a prototype), which is a very strong default model prior and pulled hands/arms/torso to dominate the frame even under an explicit no-human policy.
abstract_system_no_operator.good_pattern: Remove the operator entirely and represent the process as a self-contained abstract or mechanical system: a neural-network/data-flow graph, a prototype mid-automatic-operation, a self-contained rig - with the majority of the frame left as clean negative space rather than filled with a body.
abstract_system_no_operator.notes: This is the highest-risk containment rule in the set - technology.ai was round 3's single worst failure. Treat any archetype routed here as needing the strongest possible explicit containment language, not the baseline policy alone.

screen_non_human_content.bad_pattern: A screen/display within the scene is allowed to show generic 'story' or 'scene' content, which the model reliably fills with a human figure or character even when the physical room has no people.
screen_non_human_content.good_pattern: Constrain any in-scene screen/display content to an explicit non-human visual whitelist (galaxy, ocean horizon, clouds, abstract city lights, landscape) and forbid figurative/character/story content on it entirely - this rule applies to media INSIDE the scene, not just the physical room.
screen_non_human_content.notes: This rule generalizes to any hobby where a screen-within-the-scene could show narrative content (e.g. a future technology.streaming or arts.animation card) and should be applied proactively wherever a display surface is unavoidable.

private_environment_animal.bad_pattern: A real-animal protagonist placed in a public-facing environment (a window facing a street) still leaks small background human silhouettes even though the animal itself is fully compliant.
private_environment_animal.good_pattern: Keep the real-animal protagonist but constrain the environment to a private space only: a fenced private garden, or a home interior whose window shows only garden/plants/rain/sky, never a street.
private_environment_animal.notes: The animal itself was never the problem in any round - only the background environment. This rule should be paired with the explicit animal carve-out from object_first_rules_v2.json, not with the general containment policy alone.

swimming_hard_case_no_visible_swimmer.bad_pattern: Any narrative implying a swimmer currently in the water or having JUST passed through (a splash, a fresh entry trail, dispersing bubbles at the point of entry) still leaked a partial human body part (a foot/ankle) even under an explicit no-human policy, because the storytelling device itself implies a body.
swimming_hard_case_no_visible_swimmer.good_pattern: Use only a genuinely static empty-lane presentation: goggles and cap resting on the starting block, taut lane ropes, ambient ripples and reflections near the pool wall, water droplets - with no narrative device that implies a swimmer was just there.
validated_by: outdoors.swimming (round 3 minor fail -> round 4 redesign, explicitly called out as a special hard case in the round-4 brief)
swimming_hard_case_no_visible_swimmer.notes: This is the strictest rule in the set - it is the only one that forbids the 'aftermath' storytelling device otherwise encouraged by action_aftermath, because in this specific case the aftermath device itself was the leak vector, not the fix.

generic_structural_containment.bad_pattern: A default scene design that assumes a person is present to perform the activity, even when the archetype's own object/equipment/environment language could carry full recognition alone.
generic_structural_containment.good_pattern: Apply the general V2 non-human-protagonist policy (empty/private environment, object/equipment/environment as hero, physical traces of the activity) without a more specialized containment pattern - these archetypes have not shown the sharper, scene-specific leak vectors found in the other named rules.
generic_structural_containment.notes: This is the default/fallback rule and is expected to cover the largest number of catalog rows. It is intentionally less prescriptive than the named rules because no round has yet found a specific leak pattern requiring a bespoke fix for these archetypes.
